items.name: universal arrow from an object to a functor
items.statement_summary: Given a functor S : D -> C and an object c of C, a universal arrow from c to S is a pair <r, u> with r an object of D and u : c -> S r such that for every object d of D and every arrow f : c -> S d there exists a unique f' : r -> d with S f' o u = f (every arrow c -> S d factors uniquely through u).

items.name: universal arrow as initial object of a comma category
items.statement_summary: u : c -> S r is universal from c to S exactly when <r, u> is an initial object of the comma category (c downarrow S) (objects: arrows c -> S d). Hence a universal arrow is unique up to isomorphism in (c downarrow S), and the object r is unique up to isomorphism in D.

items.name: free vector space on a set as a universal arrow
items.statement_summary: For U : Vect_K -> Set the forgetful functor and X a set, the vector space V_X of formal K-linear combinations of X together with the insertion-of-basis map j : X -> U(V_X) is a universal arrow from X to U: every function f : X -> U(W) extends to a unique linear map f' : V_X -> W with U f' o j = f.

items.name: free algebraic constructions as universal arrows
items.statement_summary: The graph morphism P : G -> U C into the free category on a graph (Theorem II.7.1, U : Cat -> Grph) is a universal arrow; likewise the generator insertions for the free monoid on a set, the free group, the free R-module over a ring R, and the polynomial algebra over a commutative ring are universal arrows to the respective forgetful functors.

items.name: field of quotients as a universal arrow (and a non-existence example)
items.statement_summary: For an integral domain D, the pair <Q(D), j : D -> Q(D)> (field of quotients with its embedding) is a universal arrow from D to the forgetful functor Fld -> Dom_m, where Dom_m has integral domains with only monomorphisms as arrows. Contrast: over Dom (all homomorphisms of domains) no universal arrow from Z to Fld -> Dom exists, since the maps Z -> Z_p for each prime p cannot all factor through a single field.

items.name: metric-space completion as a universal arrow
items.statement_summary: With Met the category of metric spaces and metric-preserving functions (necessarily injective), and complete metric spaces the full subcategory, the completion X-bar of a metric space X gives an arrow X -> X-bar that is a universal arrow from X to the evident forgetful (inclusion) functor from complete metric spaces to Met. The uniqueness of universal arrows gives uniqueness of the completion up to a unique isomorphism.

items.name: universal element of a set-valued functor
items.statement_summary: For a category D and a functor H : D -> Set, a universal element of H is a pair <r, e> with r an object of D and e in H r such that for every pair <d, x> with x in H d there is a unique arrow f : r -> d of D with (H f) e = x.

items.name: quotient set by an equivalence relation as a universal element
items.statement_summary: For an equivalence relation E on a set S, the pair <S/E, p> (p : S -> S/E the projection onto equivalence classes) is a universal element of the functor H : Set -> Set sending each set X to the set of all functions f : S -> X with f s = f s' whenever s E s' (E-respecting functions factor uniquely through p).

items.name: quotient group as a universal element
items.statement_summary: For N a normal subgroup of a group G, the pair <G/N, p> (p : G -> G/N the coset projection) is a universal element of the functor H : Grp -> Set assigning to each group G' the set of homomorphisms f : G -> G' with f N = 1 (killing N): every such f factors as f = f' o p for a unique f'. All other properties of quotient groups (e.g. the isomorphism theorems) follow from this one universality without further mention of cosets.

items.name: tensor product of vector spaces as a universal element
items.statement_summary: For vector spaces V, V' over a field K, the tensor product V (x) V' together with the bilinear map (x) : V x V' -> V (x) V' is a universal element of the functor H = Bilin(V, V'; -) : Vect_K -> Set assigning to W the set of bilinear functions V x V' -> W. The same holds over a commutative ring with K-modules.

items.name: universal elements and universal arrows subsume each other
items.statement_summary: If * is a one-point set, any element e in H r corresponds to an arrow e : * -> H r in Ens, and a universal element <r, e> of H : D -> Set is exactly a universal arrow from * to H. Conversely, when C has small hom-sets, <r, u : c -> S r> is a universal arrow from c to S : D -> C if and only if <r, u in C(c, S r)> is a universal element of the functor H = C(c, S -) : D -> Set (acting by d |-> C(c, S d), h |-> C(c, S h)).

items.name: universal arrow from a functor to an object (couniversal arrow)
items.statement_summary: Dual notion: given S : D -> C and an object c of C, a universal arrow from S to c is a pair <r, v> with r an object of D and v : S r -> c such that for every pair <d, f> with f : S d -> c there is a unique f' : d -> r with f = v o S f'.

items.name: diagonal functor and product projections as a universal arrow
items.statement_summary: The diagonal functor Delta : C -> C x C is defined by Delta c = <c, c>. The product projections p : a x b -> a, q : a x b -> b (in Grp, Set, Cat, ...) form the pair <p, q> = a universal arrow from Delta to the object <a, b> of C x C: any f : c -> a, g : c -> b give a unique h : c -> a x b with p h = f, q h = g, i.e. <f, g> : Delta c -> <a, b> factors through <p, q>.

items.name: kernels as universals
items.statement_summary: The kernel of a homomorphism (in Ab, Grp, Rng, R-Mod, ...) is a universal - more exactly, a universal (arrow) for a suitable contravariant functor. The functor in question is not spelled out in the text.

items.name: familiar constructions as universal arrows
items.statement_summary: Interpret each of the following as a universal arrow: (a) the integral group ring of a group (better, of a monoid); (b) the tensor algebra of a vector space; (c) the exterior algebra of a vector space.

items.name: universal element of the contravariant power-set functor
items.statement_summary: Find a universal element for the contravariant power-set functor P : Set^op -> Set.

items.name: universal arrows to four forgetful functors
items.statement_summary: From any given object, find universal arrows to each of the forgetful functors: Ab -> Grp, Rng -> Ab (forget the multiplication), Top -> Set, and Set_* -> Set (pointed sets to sets).

items.name: group isomorphism theorems from universality of projections
items.statement_summary: Using only the universality of the quotient projections, prove: (a) for normal subgroups M, N of G with M contained in N, (G/M)/(N/M) is isomorphic to G/N (third isomorphism theorem); (b) for subgroups S and N of G with N normal and SN their join, SN/N is isomorphic to S/(S meet N) (second isomorphism theorem). Derive isomorphism theorems by universality.

items.name: quotient modules by universality
items.statement_summary: Show that the quotient K-module A/S (S a submodule of A) has a description by universality, and derive the module isomorphism theorems from it.

items.name: ring quotients by universality
items.statement_summary: Describe the quotient of a ring by a two-sided ideal by universality.

items.name: polynomial ring as a universal construction
items.statement_summary: Show that the construction of the polynomial ring K[x] in an indeterminate x over a commutative ring K is a universal construction.

items.name: universal arrows via natural hom-set bijections
items.statement_summary: For a functor S : D -> C, a pair <r, u : c -> S r> is universal from c to S if and only if the function sending each f' : r -> d to S f' o u is a bijection of hom-sets D(r, d) = C(c, S d), and this bijection is natural in d. Conversely, given objects r and c, any natural isomorphism D(r, -) = C(c, S -) is determined in this way by a unique arrow u : c -> S r such that <r, u> is universal from c to S.

items.name: representation of a functor; representable functor
items.statement_summary: Let D have small hom-sets. A representation of a functor K : D -> Set is a pair <r, psi> with r an object of D and psi : D(r, -) = K a natural isomorphism. The object r is the representing object; K is representable when such a representation exists. Up to isomorphism a representable functor is just a covariant hom-functor D(r, -).

items.name: representations correspond to universal arrows from a point
items.statement_summary: Let * be a one-point set and D have small hom-sets. If <r, u : * -> K r> is a universal arrow from * to K : D -> Set, then the function psi which for each object d sends f' : r -> d to K(f')(u *) in K d is a representation of K; and every representation of K is obtained in this way from exactly one such universal arrow. (Via Set(*, X) = X: representations of K are equivalent to universal elements of K.)

items.name: the Yoneda Lemma
items.statement_summary: If K : D -> Set is a functor and r an object of D (D a category with small hom-sets), there is a bijection y : Nat(D(r, -), K) = K r which sends each natural transformation alpha : D(r, -) -> K to alpha_r(1_r), the image of the identity of r under the r-component of alpha.

items.name: natural transformations between hom-functors
items.statement_summary: For objects r, s of D, each natural transformation D(r, -) -> D(s, -) has the form D(h, -) for a unique arrow h : s -> r.

items.name: naturality of the Yoneda bijection (addendum)
items.statement_summary: The Yoneda bijection is natural in both K and r: regard both sides as functors on Set^D x D, with codomain the evaluation functor E : <K, r> |-> K r and domain the functor N : <K, r> |-> Nat(D(r, -), K) (on arrows <F : K -> K', f : r -> r'> by Nat(D(f, -), F)); then y is a natural isomorphism y : N = E between the functors E, N : Set^D x D -> Set.

items.name: the Yoneda functor and its dual (full and faithful embedding)
items.statement_summary: The object function r |-> D(r, -) and arrow function (f : s -> r) |-> D(f, -) : D(r, -) -> D(s, -) define a full and faithful functor Y : D^op -> Set^D, the Yoneda functor. Its dual Y' : D -> Set^(D^op) (also faithful, sending f : s -> r to D(-, f) : D(-, s) -> D(-, r)) is the covariant version. Fullness and faithfulness follow from the corollary to the Yoneda Lemma. D must have small hom-sets for these to be defined.

items.name: Yoneda for large categories via an enlarged Ens
items.statement_summary: For D larger than allowed by small hom-sets, the Yoneda lemmas remain valid with Set replaced by any category Ens of sets for which Ens(X, Y) is the set of all functions X -> Y, provided the hom-sets of D are objects of Ens; the meaning of naturality is not altered by further enlargement of Ens (pointer to Exercise III.2.4).

items.name: arrows between representing objects
items.statement_summary: If K, K' : D -> Set have representations <r, psi> and <r', psi'> respectively, prove that to each natural transformation tau : K -> K' there is a unique arrow h : r' -> r of D with tau o psi = psi' o D(h, -) : D(r, -) -> K'.

items.name: dual (contravariant) Yoneda Lemma
items.statement_summary: State the dual of the Yoneda Lemma, with D replaced by D^op (i.e. the bijection Nat(D(-, r), K) = K r for contravariant K : D^op -> Set).

items.name: Kan's coyoneda lemma via the category of elements
items.statement_summary: (Kan; the coyoneda lemma.) For K : D -> Set, let (* down K) be the category of elements (objects: elements x in K d), Q : (* down K) -> D the projection sending x in K d to d, and for each a in D let a also denote the constant (diagonal) functor (* down K) -> D at value a. Establish a natural isomorphism Nat(K, D(a, -)) = Nat(a, Q) (natural transformations from K to the representable at a correspond to natural transformations from the constant functor a to the projection Q).

items.name: naturality unchanged by enlarging the codomain
items.statement_summary: Let E be a full subcategory of E' with inclusion J : E -> E'. For functors K, L : D -> E, prove Nat(K, L) = Nat(J K, J L).

items.name: coproduct (binary): coproduct diagram, injections, coproduct object
items.statement_summary: For the diagonal functor Delta : C -> C x C (Delta c = <c, c>, Delta f = <f, f>), a coproduct diagram is a universal arrow from an object <a, b> of C x C to Delta: an object c with injections i : a -> c, j : b -> c such that for every pair f : a -> d, g : b -> d there is a unique h : c -> d with f = h o i and g = h o j. The object c, unique up to isomorphism, is written a u b or a + b (the coproduct object); the assignment <f, g> |-> h is a bijection C(a, d) x C(b, d) = C(a u b, d) natural in d, with inverse h |-> <h i, h j>. Injections need not be injective functions.

items.name: coproduct as a bifunctor
items.statement_summary: If every pair of objects of C has a coproduct, then choosing a coproduct diagram for each pair makes u : C x C -> C a bifunctor, with h u k : a u b -> a' u b' for h : a -> a', k : b -> b' defined as the unique arrow with (h u k) o i = i' o h and (h u k) o j = j' o k.

items.name: coproducts in familiar categories
items.statement_summary: Concrete coproducts: disjoint union of sets (Set) and of spaces (Top); wedge product joining at base points (Top_*); direct sum A (+) B (Ab, R-Mod); free product (Grp); tensor product R (x) S (CRng). In a preorder P regarded as a category, the coproduct of a and b is exactly a least upper bound a v b (a <= a v b, b <= a v b, and a <= c, b <= c imply a v b <= c).

items.name: infinite (X-indexed) coproduct
items.statement_summary: For any set X regarded as a discrete category, the functor category C^X has as objects X-indexed families a = {a_x}; the diagonal Delta : C -> C^X sends c to the constant family. An X-fold coproduct diagram is a universal arrow from a family a to Delta: an object u_x a_x with injections i_x : a_x -> u_x a_x such that the assignment f |-> {f o i_x | x in X} is a bijection C(u_x a_x, c) = Prod_{x in X} C(a_x, c), natural in c. In Set: X-fold disjoint union.

items.name: copower
items.statement_summary: When all factors of an X-indexed coproduct are equal (a_x = b for all x), the coproduct u_x b is the copower X . b, satisfying C(X . b, c) = C(b, c)^X naturally in c. In Set, the copower X . Y is the cartesian product X x Y.

items.name: cokernel (in a category with a null object)
items.statement_summary: Suppose C has a null object z, so any two objects b, c have a zero arrow 0 : b -> z -> c. The cokernel of f : a -> b is an arrow u : b -> e with (i) u o f = 0 : a -> e, and (ii) whenever h : b -> c has h o f = 0, then h = h' o u for a unique h' : e -> c. In Ab, the cokernel of f : A -> B is the projection B -> B/fA; in many categories cokernels are quotient objects. In categories without a null object cokernels are unavailable, motivating coequalizers.

items.name: coequalizer of a parallel pair
items.statement_summary: Given a parallel pair f, g : a -> b in C, a coequalizer of <f, g> is an arrow u : b -> e (or the pair <e, u>) with (i) u o f = u o g, and (ii) whenever h : b -> c has h o f = h o g, then h = h' o u for a unique h' : e -> c.

items.name: coequalizer as a universal arrow (parallel-pair category)
items.statement_summary: Let the parallel-pair category (two objects, exactly two non-identity arrows from the first to the second) be denoted . => . ; an object of the functor category C^(=>) is a parallel pair <f, g> : a -> b in C, and an arrow <f, g> -> <f', g'> is a pair <h, k> making both the f-square and the g-square commute (k f = f' h, k g = g' h). The diagonal Delta : C -> C^(=>) sends c to <1_c, 1_c> and r to <r, r>. An arrow h : b -> c with h f = h g is the same as an arrow <f, g> -> Delta c, so a coequalizer <e, u> of <f, g> is exactly a universal arrow from the object <f, g> to Delta. Coequalizers of an arbitrary set of maps a -> b are defined the same way.

items.name: coequalizers in Ab, Set, Top
items.statement_summary: In Ab, the coequalizer of homomorphisms f, g : A -> B is the projection B -> B/(f - g)A onto the quotient by the image of the difference homomorphism. In Set, the coequalizer of f, g : X -> Y is the projection p : Y -> Y/E onto the quotient by the least equivalence relation E on Y containing all pairs <f x, g x> for x in X. The same construction with the quotient topology gives coequalizers in Top.

items.name: pushout of a span; fibered sum
items.statement_summary: Given f : a -> b and g : a -> c with common domain, a pushout of <f, g> is a commutative square u f = v g (u : b -> r, v : c -> r) such that for every other commutative square h f = k g built on f, g there is a unique t : r -> s with t u = h and t v = k. The vertex r, unique up to a unique isomorphism, is written b u_a c (coproduct 'over a'), called the fibered sum or (vertex of) a cocartesian square.

items.name: pushout as a universal arrow (span-shape category)
items.statement_summary: Let . <- . -> . denote the span-shape category. An object of C^(.<-.->.) is a pair of arrows with common domain; Delta c = <1_c, 1_c> is the object function of a diagonal functor Delta : C -> C^(.<-.->.). A commutative square h f = k g is exactly an arrow <f, g> -> Delta s in this functor category, and the pushout of <f, g> is the universal such arrow.

items.name: pushouts in Set, Top, Grp; amalgamated products
items.statement_summary: In Set the pushout of <f, g> always exists: the disjoint union b u c with the elements f x and g x identified for each x in a. A similar construction gives pushouts in Top (including adjunction spaces). Pushouts exist in Grp; in particular if f and g are monic in Grp, the pushout-square arrows u and v are also monic, and the vertex r is the amalgamated product of b and c.

items.name: cokernel pair
items.statement_summary: Given f : a -> b in C, the cokernel pair of f is the pushout of f with f: an object r with a parallel pair u, v : b -> r (common domain b) satisfying u f = v f, such that for any parallel pair h, k : b -> s with h f = k f there is a unique t : r -> s with t u = h and t v = k.

items.name: colimit of a functor (via the diagonal functor)
items.statement_summary: For categories C and J (J the index category, usually small, often finite), the diagonal functor Delta : C -> C^J sends c to the constant functor Delta c (value c on objects, 1_c on arrows) and f : c -> c' to the constant natural transformation. A colimit ('direct limit', 'inductive limit') diagram for F : J -> C is a universal arrow <r, u> from the object F of C^J to Delta: an object r = Colim F (Lim-> F) of C together with a natural transformation u : F -> Delta r universal among natural transformations tau : F -> Delta c. Concretely tau consists of components tau_i : F i -> c with tau_j o F u = tau_i for every arrow u : i -> j of J.

items.name: cone from a base to a vertex; limiting (universal) cone
items.statement_summary: A natural transformation tau : F -> Delta c, written tau : F -> c omitting Delta, is a cone from the base F : J -> C to the vertex c (all triangles tau_j o F u = tau_i commute). In this language a colimit of F consists of an object Colim F and a cone mu : F -> Colim F from the base F which is universal: for any cone tau : F -> c there is a unique arrow t' : Colim F -> c with tau_i = t' o mu_i for every i in J; mu is the limiting cone (or universal cone) from F.

items.name: unions of nested chains as colimits; Set is small-cocomplete (preview)
items.statement_summary: For J = omega = {0 -> 1 -> 2 -> ...} and F : omega -> Set sending every arrow to an inclusion (a nested sequence F_0 in F_1 in F_2 in ...), the union U of all F_n with the cone of inclusion maps F_n -> U is Colim F. The same interpretation of unions as colimits applies in Grp, Ab, and other familiar categories. Forward pointer (to be proved; Exercise V.1.8): for J small, any F : J -> Set has a colimit.

items.name: tensor product as coproduct of commutative rings
items.statement_summary: In the category of commutative rings, show that the diagram R -> R (x) S <- S, with maps sending r to r(x)1 and s to 1(x)s, is a coproduct diagram.

items.name: binary coproducts + coequalizers give pushouts
items.statement_summary: Prove that a category with binary coproducts and coequalizers has pushouts (the pushout of a span obtained by coequalizing the two composites into the coproduct); apply this to Set, Grp, and Top.

items.name: coequalizers in the matrix category
items.statement_summary: In the category Matr_K of matrices over a field K (from section I.2), describe the coequalizer of two parallel m x n matrices A and B, viewed as two arrows n -> m.

items.name: coproducts in Cat, Mon, Grph
items.statement_summary: Describe coproducts, showing that they exist, in the category of small categories Cat, the category of monoids Mon, and the category of graphs Grph.

items.name: quotient by an equivalence relation as a coequalizer
items.statement_summary: For an equivalence relation E on a set X, show that the usual quotient set X/E of equivalence classes can be described by a coequalizer in Set (of the two projections from E to X).

items.name: coproduct existence via representability
items.statement_summary: Show that objects a and b have a coproduct in C if and only if the functor sending c to the cartesian product of hom-sets C(a,c) x C(b,c), as a functor C -> Set, is representable.

items.name: abelian group as colimit of finitely generated subgroups
items.statement_summary: For an abelian group A, with J_A the inclusion-ordered preorder of all finitely generated subgroups of A, show that A is the colimit of the evident functor J_A -> Ab; generalize.

items.name: limit of a functor (limiting cone, inverse limit)
items.statement_summary: For categories C, J and the diagonal functor Delta : C -> C^J, a limit of F : J -> C is a universal arrow from Delta to F: an object Lim F of C together with a natural transformation v : Delta(Lim F) -> F (the limiting cone, components v_i) such that every cone tau : Delta c -> F (a family tau_i : c -> F_i with F_u compose tau_i = tau_j for each u : i -> j) factors as tau_i = v_i compose t for a unique t : c -> Lim F. A natural transformation Delta c -> F is called a cone to the base F from the vertex c. Also called limit object, inverse limit, projective limit.

items.name: uniqueness of limits up to isomorphism
items.statement_summary: As with any universal arrow, the limit object Lim F and its limiting cone v : Delta(Lim F) -> F are determined by F uniquely up to isomorphism in C.

items.name: hom-set characterization of limits and colimits (equations (2),(3))
items.statement_summary: When the relevant (co)limits exist there are isomorphisms natural in c: C(c, Lim F) is isomorphic to Nat(Delta c, F) = Cone(c, F), and Cone(F, c) = Nat(F, Delta c) is isomorphic to C(Colim F, c); i.e. the limit represents the cone functor and the colimit corepresents the cocone functor.

items.name: binary product
items.statement_summary: For the discrete category J = {1,2}, a functor is a pair of objects (a,b) and its limit is the product a x b with projection arrows p, q; the universal property is equivalent to a bijection C(c, a x b) iso C(c,a) x C(c,b) natural in c, sending h to (ph, qh); conversely given f : c -> a and g : c -> b there is a unique h = (f,g) : c -> a x b with ph = f, qh = g, the arrow with components f and g. Exists in Cat, Grp, Top, Mon; in a preorder a product is a greatest lower bound.

items.name: indexed (infinite) product over a set
items.statement_summary: For a set J viewed as a discrete category, a functor is a J-indexed family of objects a_j, a cone with vertex c is a J-indexed family f_j : c -> a_j, and a universal cone consists of the product object Prod_j a_j with projections p_j, universal: every family f_j factors as f_j = p_j compose f for a unique f : c -> Prod_j a_j (the map with components f_j). Equivalently a bijection Prod_j C(c, a_j) iso C(c, Prod_j a_j) natural in c, the left product taken in Set (small hom-sets assumed).

items.name: hom-functor preserves products
items.statement_summary: The covariant hom-functor C(c,-) carries products existing in C to products in Set (forward pointer to section V.4); products over any small index set exist in Set, Top, and Grp, where they are the familiar cartesian/direct products.

items.name: power of an object
items.statement_summary: The product of a constant J-indexed family (a_j = b for all j) is called a power and written b^J; it satisfies C(c,b)^J iso C(c, b^J) naturally in c, where the left power is taken in Set (b^J in Set being the set of all functions J -> b).

items.name: equalizer (difference kernel)
items.statement_summary: For J the parallel-pair category, a functor is a pair f, g : b -> a and a limit object is an equalizer: an arrow e : d -> b with fe = ge, universal in that any h : c -> b with fh = gh factors as h = e compose h' for a unique h' : c -> d. In Set the equalizer always exists as the subset {x in b | fx = gx} with its inclusion; in Top the same with subspace topology; in Ab it is the kernel of the difference homomorphism f - g. Equalizers of any set of parallel arrows b -> a are described similarly.

items.name: equalizers are monic
items.statement_summary: Any equalizer arrow e is necessarily a monomorphism.

items.name: pullback (fibered product, cartesian square)
items.statement_summary: For J the cospan shape, a functor is a pair f : b -> a, g : d -> a with common codomain; a cone from vertex c is a pair of arrows h : c -> b, k : c -> d making the square commute (fh = gk); a universal such cone is a commutative square with vertex the pullback b x_a d and projections p, q, such that any commuting square over the cospan factors through it by a unique r : c -> b x_a d with h = pr, k = qr. The universal square is called a pullback square or cartesian square; the vertex is the pullback, fibered product, or product over a. Origin: induced fiber maps in Top.

items.name: kernel pair
items.statement_summary: The kernel pair of an arrow f : a -> b, when it exists, is the pullback of f along itself: an object d with arrows p, q : d -> a satisfying fp = fq, such that any pair h, k : c -> a with fh = fk can be written h = pr, k = qr for a unique r : c -> d.

items.name: terminal object as limit of the empty functor
items.statement_summary: For J = 0 the empty category there is exactly one functor 0 -> C and a cone over it is just an object of C; hence a limit of the empty functor is exactly a terminal object t of C (every object has a unique arrow to t).

items.name: diagram of graph shape and its limit
items.statement_summary: With U C the underlying graph of a category C, a diagram in C of shape a graph G is a graph morphism D : G -> UC; a cone mu : c -> D is a function assigning to each object i of G an arrow mu_i : c -> D_i such that D h compose mu_i = mu_j for every graph arrow h : i -> j (a natural transformation from the constant, using composition in C but not in the domain); a limit for the diagram D is a universal such cone.

items.name: graph-shaped limits reduce to functor limits via the free category
items.statement_summary: Diagram-shaped limits give nothing essentially new: with FG the free category generated by the graph G and P : G -> U(FG) the universal diagram, every diagram D : G -> UC factors uniquely as D = U D' compose P for a functor D' : FG -> C, and limits (and limiting cones) for D' correspond exactly to those for D.

items.name: pullbacks in Set and Top
items.statement_summary: Show that in Set the pullback of f : X -> Z and g : Y -> Z is the set of pairs (x,y) with x in X, y in Y and fx = gy (with the evident projections); describe pullbacks in Top.

items.name: cartesian products are categorical products in Set and Top
items.statement_summary: Show that the usual cartesian product over an index set J, with its projections, is a categorical product in Set and in Top.

items.name: limits over a category with an initial object
items.statement_summary: If the index category J has an initial object s, prove that every functor F : J -> C has a limit, namely F(s); dualize (terminal object gives colimits by evaluation).

items.name: epi iff identity square is a pushout
items.statement_summary: In any category, prove that f : a -> b is an epimorphism if and only if the square with f twice out of a and identity arrows into b (the cokernel-pair square with both legs the identity) is a pushout.

items.name: monos are stable under pullback
items.statement_summary: In a pullback square over the cospan f : b -> a <- d : g (display (8)), show that f monic implies the opposite projection q monic.

items.name: kernel pair in Set is the induced equivalence relation
items.statement_summary: In Set, show that the kernel pair of f : X -> Y is given by the equivalence relation E = {(x,x') | fx = fx'}, with the two projection maps E -> X.

items.name: kernel pairs via products and equalizers
items.statement_summary: If C has finite products and equalizers, show that the kernel pair of f : a -> b is given by p1 e, p2 e, where p1, p2 are the projections of a x a and e is the equalizer of f p1, f p2 : a x a -> b (cf. Exercise 6); dualize.

items.name: pullback pasting lemma
items.statement_summary: For two side-by-side commutative squares: (a) if both squares are pullbacks then the outer rectangle (with composite top and bottom edges) is a pullback; (b) if the outer rectangle and the right-hand square are pullbacks, so is the left-hand square.

items.name: equalizers via products and pullbacks
items.statement_summary: Show that the equalizer of f, g : b -> a may be constructed as the pullback of the two arrows (1_b, f) : b -> b x a and (1_b, g) : b -> b x a.

items.name: pullbacks + terminal give finite products and equalizers
items.statement_summary: If C has pullbacks and a terminal object, prove that C has all finite products and all equalizers.

items.name: category with finite products
items.statement_summary: A category C has finite products when every finite list of objects c_1, ..., c_n admits a product diagram: a product object c_1 x ... x c_n with n projections p_i having the usual universal property; in particular (n = 0) C has a product of no objects, i.e. a terminal object t, and (n = 2) binary products.

items.name: diagonal map
items.statement_summary: For each object c the diagonal map delta_c : c -> c x c is defined by p1 delta_c = 1_c = p2 delta_c; the family delta is a natural transformation from the identity to the (binary product) functor.

items.name: terminal + binary products imply all finite products; canonical associator and unitors
items.statement_summary: If C has a terminal object t and a chosen binary product diagram for every pair of objects, then C has all finite products; the chosen products make x a bifunctor C x C -> C (with f1 x f2 defined by p_i (f1 x f2) = f_i p_i). For any three objects there is an isomorphism alpha_{a,b,c} : a x (b x c) iso (a x b) x c natural in a, b, c, and for any a isomorphisms lambda_a : t x a iso a and rho_a : a x t iso a natural in a; all arise by uniqueness of universals from iterated products and are called canonical. Proof: iterate binary products; dual result holds for finite coproducts (initial object as empty coproduct).

items.name: finite coproducts dually; matrix calculus coproduct-to-product
items.statement_summary: Dually a coproduct of no factors is an initial object; a coproduct diagram for m objects consists of injections i_j, and any map f from the coproduct a_1 + ... + a_m to c is uniquely determined by its m cocomponents f i_j. If C has both finite products and finite coproducts, arrows from a coproduct a_1 + ... + a_m to a product b_1 x ... x b_n are uniquely determined by the m x n matrix of arrows f_jk = p_k f i_j; in finite-dimensional vector spaces (where finite coproduct coincides with finite product) this is exactly the classical matrix of a linear transformation relative to bases.

items.name: null object and zero arrow
items.statement_summary: A null object z of C is an object that is both initial and terminal; when C has one, the zero arrow 0 : a -> b between any two objects is the composite a -> z -> b of the unique arrows through z.

items.name: canonical arrow from finite coproduct to finite product
items.statement_summary: If C has a null object plus finite products and finite coproducts, there is a canonical arrow a_1 + ... + a_n -> a_1 x ... x a_n given by the identity n x n matrix (identities on the diagonal, zero arrows elsewhere); it may be an isomorphism (Ab, R-Mod: biproducts), a proper monic (pointed topological spaces, pointed sets), or a proper epi (Grp).

items.name: naturality of the diagonal
items.statement_summary: Prove that the diagonal delta_c : c -> c x c is natural in c.

items.name: coherence of the canonical maps (pentagon and triangle diagrams)
items.statement_summary: In any category with finite products, prove that the diagrams built from the canonical alpha, rho, lambda of Proposition 1 always commute: the pentagon relating the two ways of reassociating a x (b x (c x d)) to ((a x b) x c) x d via instances of alpha and 1 x alpha, alpha x 1; and the two triangle diagrams relating alpha with lambda on t x (b x c) -> (t x b) x c and with lambda, rho on a x (t x c) -> (a x t) x c.

items.name: Cat has pullbacks; comma categories as pullbacks in Cat
items.statement_summary: (a) Prove that Cat has pullbacks (cf. Exercise II.6.5). (b) Show that the comma categories (b down C) and (C down a) arise as pullbacks in Cat (of the appropriate arrow-category and slice projections).

items.name: Cat has small coproducts
items.statement_summary: Prove that Cat has all small coproducts.

items.name: pointwise products in functor categories
items.statement_summary: If B has (finite) products, show that any functor category B^C also has (finite) products, calculated pointwise.

items.name: monoid in a category
items.statement_summary: In a category C with finite products and terminal object t, a monoid is a triple (c, mu : c x c -> c, eta : t -> c) such that the associativity square commutes (mu compose (1 x mu) equals mu compose (mu x 1) modulo the canonical associativity isomorphism alpha of III.5 Proposition 1) and the two unit diagrams commute (mu compose (eta x 1) = lambda and mu compose (1 x eta) = rho on t x c and c x t).

items.name: group in a category
items.statement_summary: A group in C (with finite products and terminal t) is a monoid (c, mu, eta) together with an arrow zeta : c -> c (right inverse) making the diagram commute: mu compose (1 x zeta) compose delta_c equals eta composed with the unique arrow c -> t, where delta_c is the diagonal.

items.name: internalization of arbitrary algebraic structures
items.statement_summary: By similar commutative diagrams one may define rings in C, lattices in C, and generally internalize any type of algebraic system defined by (finitary) operations and equational identities between them.

items.name: group objects via representable functors
items.statement_summary: If C has finite products, an object c is a group (respectively a monoid) in C if and only if the contravariant hom-functor C(-,c) : C^op -> Set is a group (respectively a monoid) in the functor category Set^(C^op). Proof: a multiplication mu on c induces one on C(-,c) via the natural isomorphism C(-,c) x C(-,c) iso C(-, c x c) followed by mu_*; conversely the Yoneda lemma produces a unique mu from any natural multiplication, and a diagram chase (using how alpha commutes with the threefold projections) shows associativity transfers both ways; remainder left as an exercise.

items.name: group objects over a base without finite products
items.statement_summary: Since Set^(C^op) always has finite products (pointwise, Exercise III.5.5), one can define objects c of C such that C(-,c) is a group in that functor category even when C itself lacks finite products (the author notes no real use of this added generality).

items.name: category of monoids in C
items.statement_summary: With C having finite products and terminal t: describe the category of monoids in C (morphisms = arrows commuting with multiplication and unit), and show it has finite products.

items.name: category of groups in C has finite products
items.statement_summary: Show that the category of groups in C (C with finite products and terminal object) has finite products.

items.name: pointwise group objects in Set^B
items.statement_summary: Show that a functor T : B -> Set is a group in Set^B if and only if each Tb (for b an object of B) is an ordinary group and each Tf (for f an arrow of B) is a morphism of groups.

items.name: groups in Grp are abelian groups
items.statement_summary: (a) For an abelian group A in Set, show its multiplication A x A -> A, unit 1 -> A, and inverse A -> A are all group morphisms (A x A with the direct product structure), so A with these structure maps is a group in Grp. (b) Prove conversely that every group in Grp has this form (the Eckmann-Hilton-style characterization).

items.name: every set-valued functor is a canonical colimit of representables
items.statement_summary: Any functor K : D -> Set from a small category D can be represented, canonically, as a colimit of a diagram of representable functors D(d,-). Proof: take as index the category of elements J = 1 down K; the functor M : J^op -> Set^D sends each object (d,x) to D(d,-) and each arrow f to the induced natural transformation f* : D(d',-) -> D(d,-); the Yoneda bijections y^{-1} : K(d) -> Nat(D(d,-), K) applied to each x yield a cone from the base M to K, shown colimiting: any cone to a vertex L : D -> Set has components y^{-1}z for elements z in L(d) (Yoneda), and setting theta_d(x) = z defines the unique mediating natural transformation theta : K -> L (naturality of theta from naturality of y^{-1}).

items.name: category of elements of a set-valued functor
items.statement_summary: For K : D -> Set, the category of elements of K is the comma category 1 down K (per II.6.(3)): objects are pairs (d, x) with d an object of D and x an element of K(d); arrows f : (d,x) -> (d',x') are the arrows f : d -> d' of D with K(f)(x) = x'. Used as the diagram shape for expressing K as a colimit of representables.

items.name: dual: contravariant set-valued functors as colimits of representables
items.statement_summary: A dual argument shows that any contravariant functor D^op -> Set (D small) can be represented as a colimit of a diagram of contravariant representable functors hom(-,d).

items.name: presheaf and the presheaf category
items.statement_summary: For C a small category, a contravariant functor F : C^op -> Set is called a presheaf (intuition: C the open sets of a space, F(U) the smooth functions on U, inclusions V in U giving restriction maps F(U) -> F(V)); the functor category Set^(C^op) of all presheaves is written C-hat. Presheaves with a matching property are sheaves (forward reference to Mac Lane-Moerdijk 1992).
